segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ paramā[48ka]nandasandohamuditaḍheṇḍhaṇo hi siddhācāryaḥ | sandhyābhāṣayā pratipādayati —
segments.translation: That very meaning the [siddha]{siddha} master [Ḍheṇḍhaṇapāda]{p-dhendhana}, delighted by the fullness of [supreme joy]{paramananda}, sets forth in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as the work of the siddha master Ḍheṇḍhaṇapāda, delighted by the fullness of supreme joy, who sets forth "that very meaning" in twilight language. The phrase seems to tie the song to the matter of the one before; he does not say more here (cp.33.m1).

flags.note: The folio mark [48ka] stands inside the word paramā[48ka]nanda (paramānanda, 'supreme joy'); it is kept in the transliteration and translated through, not rendered.

In the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) the master is tshim pa, 'satisfied, sated', by the mass (tshogs) of supreme joy, where Munidatta has mudita, 'delighted' (cp.33.m1); and sandhyābhāṣā is dgongs pa'i skad, 'language of intention', the Tibetan's usual equivalent, which reflects the sandhā/sandhyā question. 'Twilight language' follows the glossary. The Tibetan names him Te Na Te (with the agent particle: Te Na Te nas).
Munidatta's Sanskrit has Ḍheṇḍhaṇa, without -pāda (cp.33.m1); the approved form Ḍheṇḍhaṇapāda is used as the glossary requires. A variant 'Ḍheṇḍhaṇa' may be wanted (see questions).

segments.translit: ṭālata ityādi | ṭā iti ṭamālam asadrūpaṃ kāyavākcittasya ṣaṣṭyuttaraśataprakṛtidoṣaṃ yasm[i]n samaye mahāsukhacakre layaṃ gataṃ tad eva mama gṛhaṃ pārśvasthacandrasūryau ta(tha)m eva vajrajāpakrameṇa ta(na)traivāntarlī(lī)no | haṇḍīti | svakāyādhāraṃ | bhaktaṃ tasya saṃvṛtibodhicittavijñānādhirūpam | gurusaṃpradāyāt me (ma) tadupalambho 'sti ataeva nairātmarūpaṃ tayā yogīndro nityaṃ tam āviśati | punaḥ punaḥś ceti sisamāropyayati |
segments.translation: "On the [ṭāla]{tala}" and so on. Ṭā means ṭamāla, the unreal form: the fault of the hundred and sixty [natures]{prakrti} of [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}. The moment at which that has gone to dissolution in the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}: that is my [house]{house}. The [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}, standing at the side, are likewise dissolved within, right there, through the process of [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}. "[Pot]{pot}" means the receptacle of one's own [body]{body}. Its [rice]{rice} is [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, having the form of [consciousness]{vijnana}. Through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya} I have no [apprehension]{upalambha} of it. Therefore, because it has the nature of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} constantly enters it, and again and again he sets it in his [mind]{citta}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the house as the moment the fault of the hundred and sixty natures dissolves in the wheel of great bliss; the absent neighbours as moon and sun, dissolved by vajra recitation; the pot as the body; the missing rice as conventional bodhicitta, unapprehended through the guru's lineage; the daily visitor as the lord of yogis entering (cp.33.m2).

equations.en: ṭamāla, the unreal form: the fault of the hundred and sixty natures of body, speech and mind
the moment at which that fault has dissolved in the wheel of great bliss
the moon and the sun
the receptacle of one's own body
conventional bodhicitta, having the form of consciousness

flags.note: Ṭamāla, by which Munidatta explains the syllable ṭā (cp.33.m2), is left untranslated: I cannot give it a sense that fits. A guess only: it may be meant to call up tamāla, the dark-barked tree, or tamas, 'darkness'. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has DA ma la mi bden pa'i gzugs, 'ḍamala, the unreal form', and writes the syllable DA.

gurusaṃpradāyāt me (ma) tadupalambho 'sti: as printed, 'through the guru's lineage I have apprehension of it'. I read 'me na ...', 'I have no apprehension of it', taking Shastri's (ma) as standing for a negative. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the negative (bla ma'i drin gyis de la de'i dmigs pa yod pa ma yin pa'o), and only the negative fits the line's 'there is no rice' (1b) and Munidatta's next words, 'therefore ... selflessness' (cp.33.m2). Shastri's parenthesized syllables in this unit seem to mark letters to drop or alternatives; I chose by sense each time: ta(tha)m eva as tathaiva, ta(na)traiva as tatraiva, antarlī(lī)no as antarlīnau (dual, for moon and sun).

nairātmarūpaṃ tayā is read as one word, nairātmarūpatayā, 'because it has the nature of selflessness'; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supports this (bdag med pa'i ngo bo nyid de yis). The printed punaḥ punaḥś ceti sisamāropyayati makes no sense as divided; I read punaḥ punaś cetasi samāropayati, 'again and again he sets it in his mind', which the Tibetan supports (yang dang yang du sems la rtog par byed do, 'again and again he conceives it in the mind'). Both are emendations (cp.33.m2).

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no separate clause 'that is my house': after the dissolution in the wheel of great bliss it goes straight on with de nyid bdag gi khyim tshes su gnas pa zla ba nyi ma, 'the moon and sun that abide as my neighbours'. It seems to read mama gṛha-pārśvastha- as one phrase, 'standing beside my house', that is, neighbours. Shastri's gṛhaṃ, ending a clause, is kept (cp.33.m2).

vijñānādhirūpam: the element adhi is unclear (perhaps for ādi, 'consciousness and the rest'). Translated 'having the form of consciousness', as the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has (rnam par shes pa'i ngo bo). Svakāyādhāra: ādhāra can be 'support' or 'receptacle'; 'receptacle' suits a pot. The Tibetan has lus kyi gzhi, 'the base of the body', and writes the pot phru ba in the comment, khru ba in the line; it has bla ma'i drin, 'the guru's kindness', for gurusaṃpradāya (cp.33.m2).

Nityaṃ tam āviśati, 'constantly enters it', answers the line's niti ābeśī ('visitors every day', 1b): Munidatta takes ābeśī as entering (āviśati), with the lord of yogis as the one who enters. What 'it' (tam, masculine) refers to is not stated; the pot of the body or the state just described are both possible (cp.33.m2).

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ draḍhayati —
veṅgetyādi | vigatāṅga yasya sa vyaṅgaḥ | aṅgaśūnyatvena taṃ prabhāsvaraṃ boddhavyaṃ | aṅgasya ṣaḍaṅgatau sayati gacchatīti sayaḥ tad eva vāyurūpaṃ tena vyaṅgena prabhāsvareṇa vijñānaparaś coditaḥ | duhila iti | karmamudrāprasaṅgād vajrāgā[rā]d āgataṃ yad bodhicittam | yo[49]gīndrasya veṇṭam iti | mūlaṃ mahāsukhacakraṃ gacchati kim adbhutam iti |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes the same meaning firm. "The [frog]{frog}" and so on. One whose limbs (aṅga) are gone (vigata) is a vyaṅga, "limbless". Through its [emptiness]{sunyata} of limbs it is to be understood as [clear light]{prabhasvara}. Because it goes (sayati), that is, moves, with its body into the [six realms]{sadgati}, it is the [snake]{snake} (sayaḥ). That is in the form of [wind]{vayu}. By that limbless one, [clear light]{prabhasvara}, the [wind]{vayu} of [consciousness]{vijnana} is impelled. "[Milked]{milking}": the [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} that has come from the house of the [vajra]{vajra} through engagement with the [karmamudrā]{karmamudra}. "The [teat]{teat}" of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}: the [root]{root}. It goes to the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}: what a [wonder]{adbhuta}!
segments.note: Munidatta reads the frog, vyaṅga, "limbless", as clear light, and the snake (his sayaḥ, apparently for sarpaḥ, where the song prints saṃsāra) as wind, which the frog impels; so his 2a had a snake driven by the frog. The milk is bodhicitta from the vajra; the teat, the root; its going up is "what a wonder!" (cp.33.m3).

equations.en: clear light, being empty of limbs
wind (vāyurūpa), the wind of consciousness
bodhicitta come from the house of the vajra through engagement with the karmamudrā
the root, of the lord of yogis
what a wonder!

flags.note: Where Shastri's song prints saṃsāra in 2a, Munidatta glosses sayaḥ, 'that which goes', from sayati gacchati, 'it goes, moves' (cp.33.m3). Neither is a usual word; the etymology works if they stand for sarpaḥ, 'snake', and sarpati, 'creeps'. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sbrul, 'snake', both in the line and in this comment (… 'gro ba'i phyir sbrul lo). The translation renders sayaḥ as 'snake' on that basis.

What Munidatta's wording implies for 2a (cp.33.m3): the line had a snake, not saṃsāra, and the frog acts on the snake: the wind of consciousness is impelled (coditaḥ, 'urged on, driven') by the limbless frog. That fits a verb of driving or pursuing, as in the draft's 'chases'; it gives no support to the Tibetan line's 'desires' ('dod pa). He does not gloss the verb baḍhila jāa itself. The song draft is not changed.

Line 2b: Munidatta takes the song's ki not as a question but as kim adbhutam, 'what a wonder!' (cp.33.m3): for him the milked milk does go back, from the root up to the wheel of great bliss. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees (ci ste ngo mtshar ba zhes so), and its line 2b is a statement ('o ma bzhos pas nu ma la ni zhugs par 'gyur, 'the milked milk enters the teat'). The draft's 2b is a question; the reviewer may want a note there. The Tibetan comment also has the bodhicitta go 'from the root of the vajra' (rdo rje'i rtsa ba nas), where the Sanskrit says only 'the root'.

aṅgasya ṣaḍaṅgatau is unclear. I read ṣaḍgatau, 'into the six realms (destinies)', with the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ('gro ba drug tu), and take aṅgasya loosely as 'with its body'; the Tibetan has yan lag ni 'gro ba drug tu brkyang zhing 'gro ba'i phyir sbrul lo, 'because it goes stretching out its limbs into the six destinies, it is a snake', which suggests a lost word for stretching (cp.33.m3).

vijñānaparaś coditaḥ, 'the one intent on consciousness is impelled', is read vijñānapavanaś coditaḥ, 'the wind of consciousness is impelled', after the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) (rnam par shes pa'i rlung gis bskul ba). The Tibetan puts the wind in the agent case ('impelled by the wind of consciousness'), which would make the wind the driver; the Sanskrit as emended makes the frog, clear light, the driver (cp.33.m3).

vajrāgā[rā]d, 'from the house of the vajra', depends on Shastri's restored [rā]. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rdo rje'i rtse mor, 'to the tip of the vajra', which points to vajrāgra- ('vajra tip') and would make the restoration unnecessary. It also has yang dag par 'khyud pas, 'by fully embracing', for prasaṅgāt, 'through engagement with' (cp.33.m3).

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) divides aṅgaśūnyatvena differently: yan lag med pa stong pa nyid de la 'od gsal du rig par bya, 'the limbless is emptiness; that is to be known as clear light' (cp.33.m3). Vyaṅga, 'limbless', is also a Sanskrit word for 'frog', which is what lets Munidatta gloss the Old Bengali beṅga through it.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsaviśeṣam āha —
baladā ityādi | balaṃ mānasādde(de)havigrahaṃ dadātīti baladas tad eva bodhicitta[ṃ] ābhāsatrayaprastutaṃ | gāvīti yogīndrasya gṛhaṇī vandhyā nairātmā tam adhikṛtya | pīṭhakaṃ svakuliśāgre gurusaṃpradāyā(ya)t tasyābhāṣadoṣaṃ | dohanam iti niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ kriyate | sandhyātrayam iti | aharniśaṃ yogīndreṇeti |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
kuliśasaroruhasaṃjoe joiṇi manapavana mahāsuha hoi |
khane ānanda bheata ṇaha lakhalakhahīna tahi parimāṇahā |
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he states a particular [practice]{abhyasa}. "The [ox]{ox}" and so on. Because it gives (dadāti) strength (bala), that is, a bodily form, from the mind, it is the strength-giver (balada), the ox. That is [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, which has brought forth the three [appearances]{abhasa}. "[Cow]{cow}" means the [wife]{grhini} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, the [barren]{barren} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}: it refers to her. The [stool]{pitha}: at the tip of one's own [vajra]{vajra}, through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, its fault of [appearance]{abhasa}. "[Milking]{milking}" means that it is made [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}. "At the [three junctures]{three-junctures}" means day and night, by the lord of yogis. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says:
In the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, [yoginī]{yogini}, [mind and wind]{mana-pavana} become [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
In that moment, by the divisions of [joy]{ananda}, the sky, free of the marked and the mark: know its measure there.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the calving ox as bodhicitta, which brings forth the three appearances; the barren cow as Nairātmā, wife of the lord of yogis; the stool as the fault of appearance at one's vajra tip, which milking makes without intrinsic nature; the three junctures as day and night. He quotes Saraha on the union of vajra and lotus (cp.33.m4).

equations.en: bodhicitta, which gives a bodily form from the mind and brings forth the three appearances
the barren Nairātmā, wife of the lord of yogis
Nairātmā
its fault of appearance, at the tip of one's own vajra
making without intrinsic nature
day and night

citations.quoted: kuliśasaroruhasaṃjoe joiṇi manapavana mahāsuha hoi | khane ānanda bheata ṇaha lakhalakhahīna tahi parimāṇahā
citations.work: Saraha, as Munidatta names him (sarahapādāḥ); the work is not named and I have not identified the verse

flags.note: For pīṭhaka, 'stool', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'bri, a female yak, a milch animal, both here and in its line 3b ('bri ni 'jo bar byed de thun mtshams gsum): it makes the milked thing an animal, where Munidatta's word is a seat (cp.33.m4). It also has snang ba'i skyon gnyis, 'the two faults of appearance', where the Sanskrit has the singular ābhāṣadoṣa.

For gṛhaṇī (gṛhiṇī), 'wife', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has khyim du, 'in the house': rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gi khyim du mo gsham bdag med ma, 'the barren Nairātmā in the house of the lord of yogis', as if reading gṛhe. It renders tam adhikṛtya, 'with reference to her', as de la dbang du byed pa, 'takes control of her', a literal sense of adhi-kṛ (cp.33.m4).

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) explains bala as 'flesh' (ba la ni sha'o) and gives the reason 'because it gives the deha to the body' (de ha lus la ster bar byed pa'i phyir ro). That suggests its manuscript had māṃsa, 'flesh', where Shastri prints mānasāt, 'from the mind'; mānasāde(de)ha is in any case damaged, with a doubled syllable (cp.33.m4).

ābhāsatrayaprastuta: prastuta, 'brought forward, undertaken', is perhaps for prasūta, 'born'; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has snang ba gsum rab tu skyes, 'the three appearances arose'. Read with the line's calving ox, bodhicitta gives birth to the three appearances; 'which has brought forth' tries to keep both senses (cp.33.m4).

The stool sentence has no verb: pīṭhakaṃ svakuliśāgre gurusaṃpradāyāt tasyābhāṣadoṣaṃ. Both pīṭhaka and ābhāṣadoṣa are accusative, so the stool may be identified with 'its fault of appearance' (the thing milked), with 'the tip of one's own vajra' as the place; or the stool may be the vajra tip itself. 'Its' (tasya) probably refers back to bodhicitta and its three appearances. The translation keeps the bare apposition (cp.33.m4).

Saraha's Apabhraṃśa verse (cp.33.m4) is tentative, above all its second line. Joiṇi is taken as a vocative, 'yoginī'. Khane: 'in the moment' (or 'the moments', the four kṣaṇas); bheata: 'divisions' (bheda); ṇaha: 'sky' (nabha), though it could be a negative; lakhalakhahīna: 'without marked and mark' (lakṣya-lakṣaṇa); parimāṇahā: 'measure', or an imperative 'know!' (pariāṇaha). the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs: rnal 'byor dri med mchog gi bde chen 'gyur, 'stainless yoga becomes supreme great bliss', with no mind and wind; then de yi tshe na dga' ba'i dbye ba ni / de la mtshon du med pa yongs kyi tshad, 'at that time the divisions of joy: in it, beyond indication, the full measure'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena svarūpaparicayam āha —
yoso buddhītyādi | bālayogināṃ yā buddhiḥ savikalpakajñānaṃ sā paramārthavidāṃ prati guruprasaṅgān ni(ni)rupalambharūpā |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
yad idaṃ sanimittasukhaṃ tad eva mahatāṃ[49ka] jñānañ ca parihīnam iti | ato 'pi ya eva cittarājacoraḥ | adattādānaṃ karoti | sa eva bhāvavicāryamāṇa śati | tadvipakṣakaparamārtharūpaḥ | ataeva bālayogināṃ duḥsādhyaṃ paramārthasatyaṃ taiḥ duḥkhena sādhi(dhya)tam iti |
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states acquaintance with the [true nature]{svarupa}. "Whoever has [understanding]{buddhi}" and so on. The [understanding]{buddhi} of [novice yogins]{balayogin}, which is knowledge with [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}, has, for those who know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, through association with the [guru]{guru}, the form of [non-apprehension]{anupalambha}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says:
"This [bliss]{sukha} with signs: for the great ones, that very bliss, and knowledge too, is left behind."
Hence also: the very [king of mind]{king-of-mind} who is the [thief]{thief} takes what is not given. That same one, when [being]{bhava-being} is under [examination]{vicara}, has the form of the [ultimate]{paramartha}, the thief's [adversary]{vipaksa}. Therefore the ultimate truth is hard for [novice yogins]{balayogin} to accomplish: they accomplish it with difficulty.
segments.note: Munidatta reads 4a as one understanding seen two ways: conceptual knowledge for novice yogins, non-apprehension for those who know the ultimate. Nothing in his wording shows a negative in the line, as the draft's "without understanding" has. The thief is the king of mind; examined, that same mind is the ultimate, the thief's adversary (cp.33.m5).

equations.en: knowledge with conceptual thought, which for those who know the ultimate has the form of non-apprehension
the king of mind, which takes what is not given

citations.quoted: yad idaṃ sanimittasukhaṃ tad eva mahatāṃ jñānañ ca parihīnam
citations.work: Saraha, as Munidatta names him (sarahapādāḥ); the work is not named. The quotation is in Sanskrit, perhaps a rendering of a dohā

flags.note: What Munidatta's wording implies for 4a (cp.33.m5): he quotes only yoso buddhī and paraphrases the line as one understanding seen two ways, conceptual for novice yogins and non-apprehending for those who know the ultimate. The 'without' of the draft, which follows the Tibetan line (blo med pa, 'without understanding'), is compatible with his reading only as understanding without an object; his paraphrase has no negative word, so it does not show that the Bengali second half was negative. The song draft is not changed.

sa eva bhāvavicāryamāṇa śati is read as bhāve vicāryamāṇe sati, a locative absolute, 'when being (the thing) is under examination'; śati for sati is an easy slip. The glossary's sadhi entry calls śati corrupt; this reading removes the difficulty (cp.33.m5).

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads vicāryamāṇa as 'practising': de nyid kyis dngos po rnam par spyod pa dang ldan par gyur pa, 'that same one, having come to practise (or engage with) things'. Rnam par spyod pa differs from rnam par dpyod pa, 'examining', by a single letter, so this may be a Tibetan scribal slip rather than a different reading. The translation follows the Sanskrit, 'examination' (cp.33.m5).

In the Saraha quotation, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gang 'dir mtshan bcas bde ba de nyid ni / chen po rnams kyi mtshan ma yongs su zhi, 'whatever bliss here has signs, for the great ones the signs are wholly stilled'. It has mtshan ma, 'signs' (nimitta), where the Sanskrit has jñānaṃ ca, 'and knowledge', and 'stilled' for parihīna, 'left behind'. The printed Sanskrit is awkward; nimittaṃ ca may be the better reading (cp.33.m5).

A guess: Munidatta's closing words, duḥsādhya, 'hard to accomplish', and sādhita, 'accomplished', may play on the song's sādhī (4b), as if he heard it from sādh-, 'accomplish', rather than as 'guard' (cp.33.m5). He never quotes sādhī, so his sense for it is inferred: the thief's adversary, the ultimate, is the nearest thing to the draft's 'guard'.

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) takes duḥkhena, 'with difficulty', literally: don dam pa'i bden pa sdug bsngal de sdug bsngal gyis bsgrub pa, 'that suffering is accomplished by suffering'. It has rang bzhin yongs su 'jal ba, 'fully assessing the nature', for svarūpaparicaya, and so sor bla ma'i drin las, 'by the guru's kindness', for prati guruprasaṅgāt. Sādhi(dhya)tam is read sādhitam (cp.33.m5).
Jñāna in savikalpakajñāna is ordinary, conceptual cognition, so it is not marked with the glossary's jnana entry, which is defined as nondual awareness (cp.33.m5).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena svarūpabhāvam āha —
niti niti ityādi | maraṇādike sarvatra bibheti iti kṛtvā sa eva sa[ṃ]sāra (na)cittaśṛgālatulyaḥ | kalyāṇamitrādhiṣṭhānāt prabhāsvaraviśuddho bhavati | tadā yuganaddhasiṃheneha spardhāṃ karoti | īdṛśyā[ṃ] ḍheṇḍhaṇapādasya caryāyāṃ virale pakṣivikṣubdhacittaśa(sa)tatādeśe ko 'pi mahāsattvaḥ | arthāvagamaṃ kariṣyatīti || 33 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the being of the [true nature]{svarupa}. "Day after day" and so on. Because it is afraid everywhere of [death]{marana} and the like, that same one, the [mind]{citta} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}, is like a [jackal]{jackal}. Through the [blessing]{adhisthana} of the [spiritual friend]{kalyanamitra} it attains the [purity]{visuddhi} of [clear light]{prabhasvara}. Then, here, it vies with the [lion]{lion} of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}. In such a song of [conduct]{carya} by [Ḍheṇḍhaṇapāda]{p-dhendhana}, rarely, in a land where the mind is forever stirred up by partisans, will some [great being]{mahasattva} come to understand its meaning.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the jackal as the mind of saṃsāra, afraid of death everywhere. Purified in clear light through the spiritual friend's blessing, it vies with the lion of coupled union. Of the last line he says that only rarely will some great being understand the meaning of such a song (cp.33.m6).

equations.en: the mind of saṃsāra, which fears death and the like everywhere
coupled union, "the lion of coupled union"

flags.note: virale pakṣivikṣubdhacittaśa(sa)tatādeśe is obscure (cp.33.m6). Virale, 'rarely', answers the line's birale. I take pakṣin as 'partisan, one who takes sides' and read cittasatata-deśe, 'in a land where the mind is forever stirred up by partisans'. Pakṣin usually means 'bird', and virale … deśe could be 'in a lonely place, disturbed by birds'. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no partisans or birds: glu dbyangs 'di 'dra sems kyis yongs su rtogs pa nyung ste / rtag tu lta ba'i sems can chen po …, 'such a song is rarely fully understood by the mind; some great being who constantly looks (or holds a view of permanence) …'.

For spardhāṃ karoti, 'vies with', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has zung 'jug seng ge dang 'dra bar byed do, 'becomes like the lion of coupled union': emulation rather than rivalry. Its last sentence is a question ('gyur ram, 'will any great being understand the meaning?') where the Sanskrit states that some great being will (cp.33.m6).

sa[ṃ]sāra (na)citta: read saṃsāracitta, 'the mind of saṃsāra', dropping Shastri's (na); saṃsaraṇacitta, 'the wandering mind', is also possible. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no saṃsāra here, and rgyun du, 'constantly', for sarvatra, 'everywhere': 'the mind that constantly fears death and the like is like a jackal'. 'That same one' (sa eva) seems to carry on the king of mind of the previous segment (cp.33.m6).

Caryā here names the song itself, as in Caryāgīti; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has glu dbyangs, 'song'. Rendered 'song of conduct' to keep the glossary's 'conduct'. 'Purity' (visuddhi) renders the adjective viśuddha by a noun phrase, 'attains the purity of clear light' (cp.33.m6).

proposals.definition: Blessing (Sanskrit adhiṣṭhāna; Tibetan byin gyis brlabs pa): the sustaining, transforming power of a teacher or deity that enters the practitioner. Munidatta says the jackal-like mind becomes pure in clear light through the blessing of the spiritual friend (cp.33.m6). Compare self-blessing (svādhiṣṭhāna) and empowerment (abhiṣeka).
proposals.rationale: A key tantric term, not yet in the glossary, that Munidatta uses for how realization comes about (cp.33.m6); distinct from self-blessing and from empowerment. A plain match on অধিষ্ঠান or on byin gyis brlabs would also catch svādhiṣṭhāna and rang byin gyis brlabs, hence the regular expressions.

questions: Shastri's parenthesized syllables, e.g. ta(tha)m eva, me (ma), mānasāde(de)ha, sa[ṃ]sāra (na)citta: I treated them as letters to drop or as alternatives and chose by sense each time; the choices are flagged in cp.33.m2–m6. Is that the convention of the edition?

cp.33.m2: I read 'me (ma)' as a negative, 'through the guru's lineage I have no apprehension of it', with the Tibetan (… yod pa ma yin pa'o) and with the line's 'no rice'. I also emended to nairātmarūpatayā and punaḥ punaś cetasi samāropayati. Do you accept these?
cp.33.m2: Munidatta's ṭamāla is left untranslated. Do you know a sense for it, or should it stay as a bare word with a note?

cp.33.m3: Munidatta (and the Tibetan line) read 2b's ki as an exclamation, 'what a wonder!': the milk does go back. The draft's 2b is a question. Do you want a note on 2b, or a second look at the line?

cp.33.m4: my rendering of the second line of Saraha's Apabhraṃśa verse (khane ānanda bheata ṇaha lakhalakhahīna tahi parimāṇahā) is tentative; the flag gives the alternatives. Can you check it, or identify the verse?

cp.33.m5: do you accept bhāve vicāryamāṇe sati for the printed bhāvavicāryamāṇa śati? Do you think Munidatta's duḥsādhya/sādhita plays on the song's sādhī? If so, the draft's 'guard' (from the Tibetan mkhar srungs) gets no support from him.
cp.33.m6: pakṣivikṣubdhacittaśa(sa)tatādeśe: 'partisans' or 'birds'? The Tibetan does not help.

Glossary points: (a) Munidatta's Sanskrit in cp.33.m1 has Ḍheṇḍhaṇa, not Ḍheṇḍhaṇapāda; add 'Ḍheṇḍhaṇa' as a variant of p-dhendhana? (b) visuddhi 'purity' fits nouns only; add a variant 'pure' for viśuddha? (c) The weave schema has no field for the first-occurrence gloss that keep-source-first-gloss terms (siddha, ṭāla, bodhicitta, karmamudrā, vajra, Nairātmā) call for; I have relied on the glossary links and the draft's notes. Is that right?
Proposal adhisthana ('blessing'): worth an entry, or should kalyāṇamitrādhiṣṭhāna simply be translated without a link?
